discussion.speaker: Roberta METSOLA (President)
discussion.text:
The first vote is on the request by the EPP Group for an urgent decision on the temporary derogation from certain provisions of the ePrivacy Directive to combat online child sexual abuse (see minutes, item 7.1).

I give the floor first to Tomas Tobé to speak in favour of the urgent decision.

discussion.speaker: Tomas TOBÉ
discussion.text:
Madam President, dear colleagues, today's vote is not about party politics. Today's vote is not about majority tactics or strategy. Today's vote is not about shared control. It is not even about procedures. It is much more important than that. Today's vote is about deciding if we want to protect our children, or if we want to protect sexual predators.

Madam President, in March, we collectively failed to protect children. But in April, this House, together, clearly urged the Commission to come up with measures to close the legal gap that we currently have. The Commission has acted, and 26 out of 27 Member States have agreed.

Colleagues, we have a unique chance right now to send a clear signal – we care. We care about our children, and we will protect them because behind every child that is exposed on sexual abuse materials online is a victim that is never heard, and an offender that is never brought to justice. Without the interim regulation, 99 % of child abuse material goes undetected. This is unacceptable. We cannot go to summer recess knowing that our children are not protected.

So I say to all you colleagues, please take responsibility today. Vote today in favour of the urgent resolution to protect children on Thursday. And then we continue our work together on the permanent regulation. Vote to protect children.

discussion.speaker: Roberta METSOLA (President)
discussion.text: I give the floor now to Mary Khan to speak against.

discussion.speaker: Mary KHAN
discussion.text:
Frau Präsidentin! Sommer, Sonne, Massenüberwachung. So stellen sich einige EU‑Eliten den Start in die Sommerferien vor. Kurz vor der Pause soll noch schnell eine Überwachungsstruktur beschlossen werden. Und das, obwohl das Parlament bereits die Chatkontrolle abgelehnt hat. Jetzt wird derselbe Vorschlag einfach wieder aufgewärmt.

In diesem Hohen Haus der Demokratie wird offenbar so lange abgestimmt, bis das Ergebnis passt. Sie alle wissen genau, dass es für die dauerhafte Chatkontrolle keine Mehrheit gibt. Deshalb versucht man nun gemeinsam mit dem Rat, das Ganze durch die Hintertür wiederzubeleben, deshalb wählt man, wie so oft, immer wieder die Salamitaktik.

Übersetzt heißt das: Private Nachrichten sollen technisch durchsuchbar gemacht werden, Bilder, Videos und sogar Texte automatisch geprüft werden. Dass man heute versucht, das Ganze durch einen Dringlichkeitsantrag durchzubringen, zeigt doch den Geist dieses Vorhabens.

Seit 2021 versucht Ursula von der Leyen schon, Zugang zu unseren privaten Nachrichten zu bekommen. Sie selbst kann ihre SMS nicht offenlegen: Jeder weiß, was 2021 auf unserem Kontinent los war während der Corona‑Maßnahmenzeit.

Und natürlich – dieses Argument zieht nicht, ich bin selbst Mutter –, natürlich wollen wir alle Kinder schützen. Aber echter Kinderschutz beginnt nicht damit, jeden Bürger unter Generalverdacht zu stellen. Echter Kinderschutz beginnt dort, wo wirklich Täter gefährlich werden: bei harten Strafen statt Bewährung; es müssen offene Täterregister her; bei besserer Strafverfolgung und der Zerschlagung von Grooming-Gangs. Wer Kinderschänder mit Samthandschuhen anfasst, aber Millionen Bürger unter Generalverdacht stellen möchte, setzt bewusst die Prioritäten falsch.

Und an jeden Bürger: Jeder Bürger kann heute einsehen und sollte dies auch tun, welcher Abgeordnete heute dafür gestimmt hat, dass seine privaten Nachrichten künftig durchsuchbar gemacht werden. Schauen Sie genau hin! Merken Sie sich die Namen! Jeder Abgeordnete, der für diesen Dringlichkeitsantrag stimmt, stimmt auch für eine Massenüberwachung.

translation.englishText:
Madam President! Summer, sun, mass surveillance. This is how some EU elites imagine the start of the summer holidays. Shortly before the break, a monitoring structure should be decided quickly. And this despite the fact that Parliament has already rejected chat control. Now the same suggestion is simply being rehashed.

In this House of Democracy, people apparently vote until the result is correct. You all know full well that there is no majority for permanent chat control. That's why they're now trying, together with the council, to revive the whole thing through the back door, which is why, as is so often the case, they're always choosing the salami tactic.

Translated, this means: Private messages should be made technically searchable and images, videos and even texts should be checked automatically. The fact that people are trying to get the whole thing through with an urgent motion today shows the spirit of this project.

Ursula von der Leyen has been trying to get access to our private messages since 2021. She herself cannot disclose her SMS: Everyone knows what was going on on our continent in 2021 during the Corona measures period.

And of course – this argument doesn't work, I'm a mother myself – of course we want to protect all children. But real child protection does not start with placing every citizen under general suspicion. Real child protection begins where perpetrators really become dangerous: with harsh punishments instead of probation; there needs to be open registers of perpetrators; with better law enforcement and the dismantling of grooming gangs. Anyone who treats child molesters with kid gloves but wants to place millions of citizens under general suspicion is deliberately setting their priorities wrong.

And to every citizen: Every citizen can and should see today which MP voted today to make their private messages searchable in the future. Take a close look! Remember the names! Every MP who votes for this emergency motion is also voting for mass surveillance.

displayTitle: Temporary derogation from certain provisions of the ePrivacy Directive to combat online child sexual abuse
sourceTitle: Temporary derogation from certain provisions of the ePrivacy Directive to combat online child sexual abuse ***II
title: Temporary derogation from certain provisions of the ePrivacy Directive to combat online child sexual abuse

explanation: The vote was on the EU's urgent procedure to extend a temporary exception to privacy rules, allowing online services to voluntarily scan private messages for child sexual abuse material [citation:4][citation:6]. A Yes vote meant approving this specific legal basis to continue such detection efforts without immediately requiring individual judicial orders for every scan [citation:1][citation:5][citation:6].
sourceTitle: Temporary derogation from certain provisions of the ePrivacy Directive to combat online child sexual abuse ***II

discussion.speaker: Roberta METSOLA (President)
discussion.text: The next vote is on amending the decision of 18 December 2024 on setting up a special committee on the Housing Crisis in the European Union, extending its term of office and adjusting its responsibilities (see minutes, item 7.3).

displayTitle: Amending the decision of 18 December 2024 on setting up a special committee on the Housing Crisis in the European Union, extending its term of office and adjusting its responsibilities
sourceTitle: Amending the decision of 18 December 2024 on setting up a special committee on the Housing Crisis in the European Union, extending its term of office and adjusting its responsibilities
title: Amending the decision of 18 December 2024 on setting up a special committee on the Housing Crisis in the European Union, extending its term of office and adjusting its responsibilities

explanation: Amendment 4 would have changed the special committee's tasks so that when it works on simplifying housing rules, it must also maintain social and environmental standards[citation:1]. A Yes vote would have required the committee to pursue speeding up construction and renovation permits without lowering those safeguards.
sourceTitle: Amending the decision of 18 December 2024 on setting up a special committee on the Housing Crisis in the European Union, extending its term of office and adjusting its responsibilities
title: § 2, point c – Am 4

explanation: Amendment 5 would have changed the official responsibilities of the European Parliament's special committee on the Housing Crisis. A Yes vote would have added a requirement for the committee to also assess the construction sector's impact on the housing market through speculation, in addition to assessing barriers affecting the sector [citation:2][citation:3][citation:4].
sourceTitle: Amending the decision of 18 December 2024 on setting up a special committee on the Housing Crisis in the European Union, extending its term of office and adjusting its responsibilities
title: § 2, point f – Am 5

explanation: Amendment 6 would change a task of the European Parliament's special housing committee from analysing the impact of "abusive financialisation practices" to the broader "causes and impact of financialisation practices and speculation" [citation:2]. A Yes vote would have approved this wording change for the committee's work plan.
sourceTitle: Amending the decision of 18 December 2024 on setting up a special committee on the Housing Crisis in the European Union, extending its term of office and adjusting its responsibilities
title: § 2, point h – Am 6

explanation: Amendment 7 would have explicitly added tenant organisations to the list of groups the special committee must consult when organising expert meetings[citation:1]. A Yes vote would have approved that expansion, requiring the committee to include tenant perspectives alongside EU institutions, governments, non-governmental groups and economic sectors.
sourceTitle: Amending the decision of 18 December 2024 on setting up a special committee on the Housing Crisis in the European Union, extending its term of office and adjusting its responsibilities
title: § 2, point p – Am 7

explanation: Amendment 3 would have changed the special committee's mandate by replacing a reference to protecting private property with a focus on protecting the right to housing and assistance, including addressing bank foreclosures, money laundering, tenants' rights, financialisation, and speculation. A Yes vote would have approved this rewritten recital as the official statement guiding the committee's work on housing policy.
sourceTitle: Amending the decision of 18 December 2024 on setting up a special committee on the Housing Crisis in the European Union, extending its term of office and adjusting its responsibilities
title: Recital D – Am 3

explanation: The amendment would change the special committee’s focus by replacing a reference to protecting private property and fighting squatting with a priority focus on fighting criminal activities like money laundering in housing. A Yes vote would have approved that rewritten recital as the committee’s updated statement of principles.
sourceTitle: Amending the decision of 18 December 2024 on setting up a special committee on the Housing Crisis in the European Union, extending its term of office and adjusting its responsibilities
title: Recital D – Am 1

sourceTitle: Air passenger rights ***III
title: Air passenger rights

A Yes vote would have approved this final negotiated version of the updated rules for air travellers across the European Union.
sourceTitle: Air passenger rights ***III
title: Andrey Novakov – Joint text

discussion.speaker: Roberta METSOLA (President)
discussion.text: The next vote is on the coordination of social security systems (see minutes, item 7.8).

sourceTitle: Coordination of social security systems ***I
title: Coordination of social security systems

explanation: Amendment 209 would have required, for most unemployed people, that they have worked and contributed to the unemployment system in a member state for at least one continuous month before that state must pay their benefits. A Yes vote would have approved this new one-month work rule as part of the updated EU social security coordination law.
sourceTitle: Coordination of social security systems ***I
title: Gabriele Bischoff – Provisional agreement – Am 209

discussion.speaker: Roberta METSOLA (President)
discussion.text: The next vote is on temporary support and payment of advances regarding the increased fertiliser prices due to the Middle East crisis (see minutes, item 7.9).

displayTitle: Temporary support and payment of advances regarding the increased fertiliser prices due to the Middle East crisis
sourceTitle: Temporary support and payment of advances regarding the increased fertiliser prices due to the Middle East crisis ***I
title: Temporary support and payment of advances regarding the increased fertiliser prices due to the Middle East crisis

explanation: This vote concerned a proposed European Union regulation to create a new exception for providing farmers with temporary financial aid and more flexible advance payments to address higher fertiliser costs linked to the Middle East crisis[citation:1][citation:3][citation:11]. A Yes vote would have approved that proposal, allowing Member States to use these measures to support affected agricultural producers.
sourceTitle: Temporary support and payment of advances regarding the increased fertiliser prices due to the Middle East crisis ***I
title: After recital 2 – Am 1

explanation: The policy change would have affected farmers by increasing the advance payment rate of their direct agricultural subsidies from 70% to 75%, making the funds available immediately after application instead of waiting until 16 October. A Yes vote would have approved this temporary amendment to the Common Agricultural Policy to help farmers purchase fertiliser for the next planting season, as proposed by the European Commission[citation:1][citation:10].
sourceTitle: Temporary support and payment of advances regarding the increased fertiliser prices due to the Middle East crisis ***I
title: Commission proposal

discussion.speaker: Roberta METSOLA (President)
discussion.text: The next vote is on international road passenger transport services by coach and bus in the border regions: cabotage operations between Austria and Switzerland (see minutes, item 7.10).

displayTitle: International road passenger transport services by coach and bus in the border regions: cabotage operations between Austria and Switzerland
sourceTitle: International road passenger transport services by coach and bus in the border regions: cabotage operations between Austria and Switzerland ***I
title: International road passenger transport services by coach and bus in the border regions: cabotage operations between Austria and Switzerland

explanation: A Yes vote would have empowered Austria to change its bilateral road transport agreement with Switzerland, specifically to allow coach and bus companies to pick up and drop off passengers within the other country's border region during an international trip. This approval would have granted Austria the legal authority to negotiate and conclude that specific amendment to its existing treaty with Switzerland.
sourceTitle: International road passenger transport services by coach and bus in the border regions: cabotage operations between Austria and Switzerland ***I
title: Elissavet Vozemberg-Vrionidi – Commission proposal and amendments

discussion.speaker: Roberta METSOLA (President)
discussion.text: The next vote is on draft amending budget no 1/2026: entering the surplus of the financial year 2025 (see minutes, item 7.11).

displayTitle: Draft amending budget No 1/2026: entering the surplus of the financial year 2025
sourceTitle: Draft amending budget No 1/2026: entering the surplus of the financial year 2025
title: Draft amending budget No 1/2026: entering the surplus of the financial year 2025

explanation: The European Parliament voted on entering the 2025 budget surplus into the 2026 budget, affecting EU funds and the budget obligations of member states. A Yes vote would have approved the Council’s position to reduce national contributions by the surplus amount.
sourceTitle: Draft amending budget No 1/2026: entering the surplus of the financial year 2025
title: Andrzej Halicki – § 7

explanation: Amendment 4 would have added a statement to the report on the 2025 budget surplus, recalling that the EU should focus on collecting existing revenue more effectively rather than creating new taxes or charges [citation:1][citation:2][citation:12]. A Yes vote would have approved inserting this specific reminder into the Parliament's formal position on the draft amending budget [citation:1][citation:9][citation:12].
sourceTitle: Draft amending budget No 1/2026: entering the surplus of the financial year 2025
title: Andrzej Halicki – After § 7 – Am 4

explanation: A Yes vote would add to the record that the European Public Prosecutor's Office's 2025 report found fraud affecting VAT and customs duties caused an estimated €45.01 billion in damage, and that the EU should improve customs controls and revenue collection rather than introduce new taxes on citizens and businesses.
sourceTitle: Draft amending budget No 1/2026: entering the surplus of the financial year 2025
title: Andrzej Halicki – After § 7 – Am 5

explanation: NO_RESULTThis amendment would have added a new section to the resolution on the 2025 surplus budget, stating that the EU should prioritize stopping existing revenue losses from fraud and weak customs controls rather than creating new taxes or fees for citizens and businesses [citation:1]. A Yes vote would have approved this language, formally recording the Parliament's position that better enforcement of current rules is the preferred way to protect the budget.
sourceTitle: Draft amending budget No 1/2026: entering the surplus of the financial year 2025
title: Andrzej Halicki – After § 7 – Am 6

displayTitle: Final vote on the motion for a resolution
explanation: Draft amending budget No 1/2026 would enter the €3.2 billion surplus from the 2025 financial year into the 2026 EU budget, reducing member states’ contribution payments. A Yes vote meant approving this surplus entry and the accompanying budgetary adjustments as proposed by rapporteur Andrzej Halicki.
sourceTitle: Draft amending budget No 1/2026: entering the surplus of the financial year 2025
title: Andrzej Halicki – Motion for a resolution (as a whole)

sourceTitle: Mobilisation of the European Globalisation Adjustment Fund: Application EGF/2026/000 TA 2026 - Technical assistance at the initiative of the Commission

discussion.speaker: Roberta METSOLA (President)
discussion.text: The next vote is on the financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025 (see minutes, item 7.13).

discussion.speaker: Jorge BUXADÉ VILLALBA
discussion.text:
Señora presidente, la señora Nadia Calviño, exministra de Sánchez y ahora a la cabeza del Banco Europeo de Inversiones, anunció en redes sociales la asignación de 365 millones EUR para carreteras y ferrocarriles de Marruecos.

Por eso, nosotros creemos importante incluir la siguiente enmienda: Lamenta la asignación por parte del Banco Europeo de Inversiones de 365 millones EUR para reforzar la resiliencia y la seguridad de las redes viarias y ferroviarias de Marruecos, tal y como anunció la presidenta del Banco, Nadia Calviño, el 30 de junio de 2026.

Recuerda que estos recursos financieros deberían destinarse prioritariamente a mejorar las infraestructuras de transporte dentro de la Unión, especialmente a la luz de los graves accidentes ferroviarios ocurridos en los últimos años, que han puesto de manifiesto las deficiencias en el mantenimiento y la modernización de las infraestructuras de transporte en varios Estados miembros.

Considera que dicha financiación no se ajusta a la misión principal del Banco, establecida en el artículo 309 del Tratado de Funcionamiento, consistente en contribuir al desarrollo equilibrado y constante del mercado interior en interés de la Unión.

translation.englishText:
Madam President, Mrs. Nadia Calviño, Sánchez's former minister and now head of the European Investment Bank, announced on social media the allocation of €365 million for roads and railways in Morocco.

For this reason, we believe it is important to include the following amendment: Regrets the allocation by the European Investment Bank of EUR 365 million to strengthen the resilience and safety of Morocco's road and rail networks, as announced by the President of the Bank, Nadia Calviño, on June 30, 2026.

Recalls that these financial resources should be allocated as a priority to improving transport infrastructure within the Union, especially in light of the serious railway accidents that have occurred in recent years, which have highlighted deficiencies in the maintenance and modernization of transport infrastructure in several Member States.

Considers that such financing does not comply with the main mission of the Bank, established in Article 309 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the Bank, which consists of contributing to the balanced and constant development of the internal market in the interest of the Union.

Recuerda que estos recursos financieros deberían destinarse prioritariamente a mejorar las infraestructuras de transporte dentro de la Unión, especialmente a la luz de los graves accidentes ferroviarios ocurridos en los últimos años, que han puesto de manifiesto las deficiencias en el mantenimiento y la modernización de las infraestructuras de transporte en varios Estados miembros.

displayTitle: Financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025
sourceTitle: Financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025
title: Financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025

explanation: A Yes vote would have added a new opening paragraph to the report stating that the European Investment Bank's primary goals should be social and territorial cohesion, with funding prioritised for public projects meeting Member States' needs, and that its activities should not be subordinate to competitiveness logic or diverted to militarisation.
sourceTitle: Financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025
title: Joachim Streit – Before § 1 – Am 3/1

explanation: Amendment 3 would have directed the European Investment Bank to prioritise funding for public projects that meet national development goals and support social cohesion, jobs, public services, housing and energy sovereignty, while prohibiting its money from being used for militarisation[citation:1][citation:3][citation:6]. A Yes vote would have approved this legally non-binding parliamentary instruction to the EIB for its future lending policies[citation:5].
sourceTitle: Financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025
title: Joachim Streit – Before § 1 – Am 3/2

explanation: A Yes vote would have added a new instruction to the European Parliament's annual report on the European Investment Bank (EIB). This would have required the EIB to act only as a last-resort lender for genuine market failures, and warned against using the EIB for EU budget purposes or expanding its defence role without full parliamentary oversight and respect for national sovereignty.
sourceTitle: Financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025
title: Joachim Streit – After § 5 – Am 11

explanation: Amendment 12 would have warned against using the European Investment Bank to effectively pool national debts or fund EU budgets outside the normal budget process. A Yes vote would have approved this warning and added it to the Parliament's report.
sourceTitle: Financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025
title: Joachim Streit – After § 6 – Am 12

explanation: The amendment would change the resolution so that it first calls on the European Commission to urgently propose extending the Recovery and Resilience Facility’s implementation period until at least 31 August 2028. A Yes vote would have approved adding this explicit new deadline request to the text before the rest of the paragraph.
sourceTitle: Financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025
title: Joachim Streit – § 8 – Am 4

explanation: A Yes vote would have added a requirement for the European Investment Bank to use technology-neutral criteria, including life-cycle carbon intensity and grid stability, when financing low-carbon energy projects like nuclear energy, while respecting each Member State's right to choose its own energy mix.
sourceTitle: Financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025
title: Joachim Streit – § 12 – Am 6

explanation: Amendment 7 would have directed the European Investment Bank to publicly share lessons from its nearly €943 million in financing to Northvolt AB and to strengthen project checks after Northvolt's bankruptcy [citation:7][citation:11]. A Yes vote would have approved requiring the EIB to report on late payments and borrower failures across its portfolio as standard practice.
sourceTitle: Financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025
title: Joachim Streit – After § 13 – Am 7

explanation: The European Parliament would have called on the European Investment Bank to use technology-neutral criteria—including life-cycle carbon intensity and grid stability—when financing low-carbon energy projects, which would include nuclear energy while respecting each Member State's right to choose its own energy mix. A Yes vote would have approved adding this requirement to the Parliament's official position on the EIB's annual report.
sourceTitle: Financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025
title: Joachim Streit – § 15 – Am 8

explanation: Amendment 5 would have changed the European Parliament’s position on EIB resources by ruling out their use for military funding and instead directing them toward tackling the cost of living and upholding the right to affordable housing for all[citation:1][citation:11]. A Yes vote would have been a vote to approve this specific amendment and its restrictions on EIB resources[citation:6].
sourceTitle: Financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025
title: Joachim Streit – After § 19 – Am 5

explanation: Amendment 9 would have added a new obligation for the European Investment Bank to report annually on its progress in removing the remaining funding restrictions for defence and security projects. A Yes vote would have approved this requirement for the EIB to produce that report.
sourceTitle: Financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025
title: Joachim Streit – § 21 – Am 9

explanation: A Yes vote would have added a new passage to the European Parliament’s report requiring the European Investment Bank to act only as a last-resort lender, avoiding any expansion that crowds out private money or replaces national investment choices. It also would have insisted that any future increase in the Bank’s role be fully scrutinised by Parliament and that defence financing respect each Member State’s control over its own military procurement and industrial strategy.
sourceTitle: Financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025
title: Joachim Streit – After § 21 – Am 13

explanation: The European Parliament votes on urging EU Member States to change the European Investment Bank's rules so it can fund weapons and ammunition, not just dual-use technologies. A Yes vote would have formally called on national governments to make that change to support Europe's defence industry.
sourceTitle: Financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025
title: Joachim Streit – After § 25 – Am 1

explanation: This amendment would have directed the European Investment Bank to use technology-neutral criteria like life-cycle carbon intensity when financing low-carbon energy projects, including nuclear power, while respecting each country's right to choose its own energy mix. A Yes vote would have added this as a formal request in Parliament's annual report on the bank's activities.
sourceTitle: Financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025
title: Joachim Streit – After § 25 – Am 10

displayTitle: Final vote on the motion for a resolution
explanation: This vote was on the non-legislative resolution assessing the European Investment Bank Group’s 2025 activities. A Yes vote meant approving Parliament’s final position on the EIB’s performance, strategic priorities, and financial operations.
sourceTitle: Financial activities of the European Investment Bank Group – annual report 2025
title: Joachim Streit – Motion for a resolution (as a whole)

discussion.speaker: Roberta METSOLA (President)
discussion.text: The next vote is on the recommendation on the changing geopolitical situation in East Asia and the need for closer cooperation with like-minded partners in the region (see minutes, item 7.14).

displayTitle: Recommendation on the changing geopolitical situation in East Asia and the need for closer cooperation with like-minded partners in the region
sourceTitle: Recommendation on the changing geopolitical situation in East Asia and the need for closer cooperation with like-minded partners in the region
title: Recommendation on the changing geopolitical situation in East Asia and the need for closer cooperation with like-minded partners in the region

explanation: Amendment 1 would have added a new instruction for the EU and its member states, the High Representative, the Commission, and the Council. A Yes vote would have required them to conduct East Asia relations to promote UN principles like sovereignty and non-interference, while also avoiding confrontation, interference, and destabilisation, including against China.
sourceTitle: Recommendation on the changing geopolitical situation in East Asia and the need for closer cooperation with like-minded partners in the region
title: Adam Bielan – § 1, before point a – Am 1

explanation: A Yes vote would have approved a new paragraph calling for reversing recent weakening of the EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (2024/1760) to strengthen its scope and enforceability, specifically to combat forced labour and social dumping in South-East Asian supply chains [citation:4].
sourceTitle: Recommendation on the changing geopolitical situation in East Asia and the need for closer cooperation with like-minded partners in the region
title: Adam Bielan – § 1, after point d – Am 6

explanation: The EU would have been called on to carry out a new human rights impact assessment for the EU-Philippines free trade agreement negotiations [citation:1]. A Yes vote would have approved adding this obligation to the European Parliament's official recommendation on East Asia.
sourceTitle: Recommendation on the changing geopolitical situation in East Asia and the need for closer cooperation with like-minded partners in the region
title: Adam Bielan – § 1, after point d – Am 7

explanation: The European Parliament would have required EU officials to conduct relations with China based on mutual respect, the One China principle, and non-interference in China's internal affairs. A Yes vote would have approved adding this instruction to the EU's official policy recommendations.
sourceTitle: Recommendation on the changing geopolitical situation in East Asia and the need for closer cooperation with like-minded partners in the region
title: Adam Bielan – § 1, after point h – Am 2

explanation: A Yes vote would add language to a European Parliament report highlighting the EU’s growing trade deficit with Vietnam, Vietnam’s lack of progress on labour rights and ratification of a key trade union convention, and human rights concerns in the Philippines. It would also call for reversing the weakening of the EU’s corporate due diligence law and for a new human rights impact assessment on EU-Philippines trade talks.
sourceTitle: Recommendation on the changing geopolitical situation in East Asia and the need for closer cooperation with like-minded partners in the region
title: Adam Bielan – After recital Y – Am 3

explanation: Amendment 4 would have added a new paragraph to the report, stating that EU-Philippines free trade talks restarted without a required human rights impact assessment, despite a European Ombudsman ruling that the Commission’s failure to do this for the EU-Vietnam deal was maladministration. A Yes vote would have approved adding this criticism of the Commission’s procedure to the Parliament’s official stance.
sourceTitle: Recommendation on the changing geopolitical situation in East Asia and the need for closer cooperation with like-minded partners in the region
title: Adam Bielan – After recital Y – Am 4

explanation: Amendment 5 would have added a new section to the resolution stating that the European Commission resumed free trade agreement talks with the Philippines in March 2024 despite continued human rights issues under President Marcos Jr., noting increased political persecution and enforced disappearances. A Yes vote would have approved adding this critical language to the official parliamentary text.
sourceTitle: Recommendation on the changing geopolitical situation in East Asia and the need for closer cooperation with like-minded partners in the region
title: Adam Bielan – After recital Y – Am 5

displayTitle: Final vote on the motion for a resolution
explanation: NO_RESULTThe recommendation aims to strengthen the European Parliament’s role in shaping EU foreign policy toward East Asia by calling for coordinated action with regional partners on geopolitical challenges. A Yes vote would have approved the resolution as a whole, endorsing its political objectives and specific proposals for deepening cooperation with like-minded countries in the region.
sourceTitle: Recommendation on the changing geopolitical situation in East Asia and the need for closer cooperation with like-minded partners in the region
title: Adam Bielan – Motion for a resolution (as a whole)

discussion.speaker: Roberta METSOLA (President)
discussion.text: The next vote is on competition policy – annual report 2025 (see minutes, item 7.15).

sourceTitle: Competition policy – annual report 2025
title: Competition policy – annual report 2025

explanation: A Yes vote would have added a new paragraph to the non-binding resolution, asserting that competition policy should not obstruct active industrial strategies and that EU rules should not prevent Member States from making necessary public investments for climate adaptation and industrial transformation [citation:4].
sourceTitle: Competition policy – annual report 2025
title: Stéphanie Yon-Courtin – After § 3 – Am 1

explanation: The amendment would have added a new passage to the European Parliament’s annual competition report. It states that public ownership and public control of companies that are strategically important for a climate-neutral economy are vital, and calls on the European Commission and EU countries to create a framework to make such public ownership and control easier in those economic sectors. A Yes vote would have approved adding that text to the report.
sourceTitle: Competition policy – annual report 2025
title: Stéphanie Yon-Courtin – After § 3 – Am 2

explanation: Amendment 10 would have invited EU member countries to replace subsidy-based support with public procurement contracts reserved for European companies, aiming to help them compete against US and Chinese corporations[citation:AM10]. A Yes vote would have approved adding this invitation as a new paragraph to the Parliament's annual competition policy report.
sourceTitle: Competition policy – annual report 2025
title: Stéphanie Yon-Courtin – After § 9 – Am 10

explanation: Amendment 3 would have added a new paragraph to the resolution stating that corporate profits have been a major cause of inflation and that profit-driven inflation should be countered with measures like windfall taxes, price controls, or antitrust action. A Yes vote would have approved calling on EU countries and the Commission to immediately introduce permanent windfall profit taxes in all sectors and to redistribute that revenue to low-income households.
sourceTitle: Competition policy – annual report 2025
title: Stéphanie Yon-Courtin – After § 13 – Am 3

explanation: Amendment 4 would have added a new paragraph to the report stressing that the European Commission and national competition authorities need to be especially vigilant about excessive profits in food and energy supply chains. A Yes vote would have approved this addition, calling for heightened scrutiny of companies with significant market power in essential goods.
sourceTitle: Competition policy – annual report 2025
title: Stéphanie Yon-Courtin – After § 41 – Am 4

explanation: Amendment 5 would have added a new paragraph to the report stating that recent consolidation in the EU telecoms industry tends to lead to higher prices and lower-quality services for consumers [citation:2]. A Yes vote would have approved this addition.
sourceTitle: Competition policy – annual report 2025
title: Stéphanie Yon-Courtin – After § 45 – Am 5

explanation: A Yes vote would have added a new paragraph to the European Parliament's annual report on competition policy. It would have stated that competition rules should not block EU or national industrial strategies backed by strong public investment, particularly for fighting inequality, decarbonising industry, and adapting to climate disasters [citation:1].
sourceTitle: Competition policy – annual report 2025
title: Stéphanie Yon-Courtin – After § 46 – Am 6

explanation: Amendment 7 sought to add a new paragraph to the resolution, stating that competition policy should not block active industrial strategy, and that EU countries must be free to make public investments needed for climate adaptation and industrial transformation, even if this affects competition rules. A Yes vote would have approved adding this statement to the report.
sourceTitle: Competition policy – annual report 2025
title: Stéphanie Yon-Courtin – After § 50 – Am 7

explanation: A Yes vote would have added a new paragraph to the report expressing concern that EU aid frameworks linked to the Green Deal have raised energy costs and regulatory burdens, arguing such policies shift costs to consumers and businesses while expanding EU bureaucracy. [citation:1]
sourceTitle: Competition policy – annual report 2025
title: Stéphanie Yon-Courtin – After § 50 – Am 12

explanation: A Yes vote would approve amending report paragraph 23 to call on the European Commission to use its market investigation to adjust Digital Markets Act obligations for cloud services, removing switching barriers. This would target major providers’ practices to enable easier multi-cloud use and provider changes.
sourceTitle: Competition policy – annual report 2025
title: Stéphanie Yon-Courtin – § 54

displayTitle: Final vote on the motion for a resolution
explanation: A Yes vote would have approved the European Parliament's own-initiative resolution on the 2025 annual report on competition policy, specifically the final text as presented by rapporteur Stéphanie Yon-Courtin in document A10-0171/2026. This would have set out the Parliament's official positions and recommendations to the European Commission and Member States regarding the future application and enforcement of EU competition rules, affecting businesses, consumers, and national authorities.
sourceTitle: Competition policy – annual report 2025
title: Stéphanie Yon-Courtin – Motion for a resolution (as a whole)

discussion.speaker: Roberta METSOLA (President)
discussion.text: The next vote is on a coherent tax framework for the EU's financial sector (see minutes, item 7.16).

discussion.speaker: Matthias ECKE
discussion.text:
Madam President, colleagues, we cannot carry on like this. This is not sustainable. Our financial sector taxation system needs reform. Europe needs more investment for our digital and green transitions to strengthen our security and to foster investment. We need a deeper integrated financial market, but our taxation system has not kept up with that challenge. The VAT exemption on financial services dates back to 1977. This is nearly 50 years and it was designed for an entirely different financial system. Today, it creates distortions and it undermines our single market.

There is no simple solution for that. This is why this report is proposing no specific recipe, but it calls on the Commission to thoroughly investigate the matter and to propose a coherent framework. And to be honest, colleagues, I expect ambition. I expect the Commission to also assess the role that financial transaction tax and windfall taxes can play in such a framework. We should also take a hard look on whether national tax regimes for the financial sector contribute to harmful tax competition in the European Union and sustain tax havens.

Colleagues, the shortcomings of the current system have led to more than 90 different national sectoral taxations – more than 90 – across the Union. So, this patchwork creates unnecessary complexity and bureaucracy. It distorts the single market and it ultimately weakens European competitiveness. After almost 50 years, it's time for a change. It's time to modernise. I want you to be part of that modernisation. I am asking for your support.

displayTitle: A coherent tax framework for the EU's financial sector
sourceTitle: A coherent tax framework for the EU's financial sector
title: A coherent tax framework for the EU's financial sector

explanation: A Yes vote would have rewritten the European Parliament’s instructions to the European Commission, changing a demand for a review into a formal welcome of the Commission’s June 2026 study on financial-sector taxation. It would have explicitly added the study’s findings to the official text, confirming that the VAT exemption causes hidden tax burdens, complexity, and misalignment with EU savings and investment goals, while still asking the Commission to consider reforms.
sourceTitle: A coherent tax framework for the EU's financial sector
title: Matthias Ecke – § 27 – Am 3

explanation: Amendment 4 would have changed the European Parliament's position on the withdrawn EU financial transaction tax proposal. A Yes vote would have approved text calling on the European Commission to ensure any new tax framework includes a concrete plan to address the gap left by the withdrawal and to be no less ambitious than the original FTT proposal.
sourceTitle: A coherent tax framework for the EU's financial sector
title: Matthias Ecke – § 33 – Am 4

explanation: A Yes vote would have added a new paragraph to the European Parliament's report, directly calling on the European Commission to create a new EU law for temporary taxes on exceptionally high profits in the financial sector during major economic crises. It would have required the Commission to propose this new legislation, which would apply coordinated temporary windfall taxes across EU member states to ensure the sector makes a fair contribution.
sourceTitle: A coherent tax framework for the EU's financial sector
title: Matthias Ecke – § 34 – Am 5

explanation: Amendment 6/rev would add a new paragraph to the report stating that financial sector tax rules should not be used to attract profits through tax-driven profit shifting rather than genuine economic activity[citation:1][citation:3]. A Yes vote would have approved adding this language to the Parliament's position on creating a fairer tax framework for the EU financial sector[citation:1][citation:3].
sourceTitle: A coherent tax framework for the EU's financial sector
title: Matthias Ecke – § 35 – Am 6

displayTitle: Final vote on the motion for a resolution
explanation: The European Parliament voted on its own non-binding opinion calling on the European Commission to propose new EU-wide taxes on financial transactions and on the financial sector’s profits and capital gains. A Yes vote would have meant the Parliament officially adopting that full set of recommendations to the Commission.
sourceTitle: A coherent tax framework for the EU's financial sector
title: Matthias Ecke – Motion for a resolution (as a whole)

discussion.speaker: Roberta METSOLA (President)
discussion.text: The next vote is on a new strategy for media literacy and digital learning (see minutes, item 7.17).

discussion.speaker: Marcos ROS SEMPERE
discussion.text:
Señora presidenta, durante mucho tiempo vimos la expansión de internet y de las redes sociales con optimismo. Pensábamos que la información circularía libre y que la conversación pública sería más abierta. Sin embargo, el espacio digital que nos atraviesa por completo ha cambiado radicalmente y ese optimismo se ha nublado. La concentración de poder en pocas manos, la opacidad y un modelo de negocio basado en la adicción permanente ha transformado profundamente ese ecosistema. La desinformación circula con facilidad, los contenidos manipulados se multiplican y la inteligencia artificial ha acelerado y multiplicado este efecto.

Conocer cómo funciona este nuevo mundo debe ser hoy una prioridad democrática. Hace décadas, entendimos que no existía la ciudadanía plena sin saber leer y escribir. Hoy, nos ocurre algo parecido: en la era digital, nadie puede ejercer plenamente sus derechos si no distingue la realidad de la desinformación, si no reconoce una manipulación generada por inteligencia artificial o si no entiende cómo funcionan los algoritmos. Y si nuestra ciudadanía no tiene esas herramientas, nuestras democracias no están preparadas para esta nueva era digital.

Señorías, ningún Estado miembro puede afrontar este desafío por sí solo. Por eso, hoy votamos implementar una nueva estrategia de alfabetización mediática y de aprendizaje digital para toda Europa. Una estrategia que reconozca competencias como básicas y esenciales para toda la ciudadanía, a cualquier edad y a lo largo de toda la vida, especialmente para niños, niñas y adolescentes. Servirá para su protección frente al acoso, los contenidos inapropiados y el diseño adictivo, también para nuestros mayores y el conjunto de la ciudadanía, porque nadie puede ser libre en un entorno digital que no entiende.

La alfabetización mediática y digital es una necesidad democrática y hoy enviamos un mensaje claro. Gracias por su voto.

translation.englishText:
Madam President, for a long time we viewed the expansion of the internet and social networks with optimism. We thought that information would circulate freely and that public conversation would be more open. However, the digital space that completely crosses us has changed radically and that optimism has been clouded. The concentration of power in a few hands, opacity and a business model based on permanent addiction has profoundly transformed that ecosystem. Misinformation circulates easily, manipulated content multiplies and artificial intelligence has accelerated and multiplied this effect.

Knowing how this new world works must be a democratic priority today. Decades ago, we understood that there was no such thing as full citizenship without knowing how to read and write. Today, something similar happens to us: in the digital age, no one can fully exercise their rights if they do not distinguish reality from misinformation, if they do not recognize manipulation generated by artificial intelligence or if they do not understand how algorithms work. And if our citizens do not have these tools, our democracies are not prepared for this new digital age.

Ladies and gentlemen, no Member State can meet this challenge alone. That is why today we voted to implement a new media literacy and digital learning strategy for all of Europe. A strategy that recognizes competencies as basic and essential for all citizens, at any age and throughout life, especially for boys, girls and adolescents. It will serve to protect them against harassment, inappropriate content and addictive design, also for our elders and the general public, because no one can be free in a digital environment that they do not understand.

Media and digital literacy is a democratic necessity and today we send a clear message. Thank you for your vote.

displayTitle: A new strategy for media literacy and digital learning
sourceTitle: A new strategy for media literacy and digital learning
title: A new strategy for media literacy and digital learning

explanation: Amendment 1 would have changed the EU's position on media literacy by adding a warning that it must not be used within the EU Democracy Shield initiative to promote a biased view of information [citation:2]. A Yes vote would have approved this amendment, thereby directing the European Parliament to express concern that such measures could marginalise opinions critical of EU policies.
sourceTitle: A new strategy for media literacy and digital learning
title: Marcos Ros Sempere – § 3 – Am 1

explanation: The European Parliament’s own-initiative report on media literacy would have mandated that EU countries and the European Commission allocate specific funding and technical support to develop national media literacy programmes for all age groups. A Yes vote would have approved this binding obligation for EU institutions and member states to act.
sourceTitle: A new strategy for media literacy and digital learning
title: Marcos Ros Sempere – § 3

explanation: A Yes vote would have changed paragraph 6 of the resolution to state that acquiring media literacy and digital skills is primarily the responsibility of parents and legal guardians, followed by the national school systems, and is not a lifelong process supervised by EU institutions. It would have explicitly warned against an overly broad EU interpretation of this oversight and recalled that education remains a national competence under the principle of subsidiarity.
sourceTitle: A new strategy for media literacy and digital learning
title: Marcos Ros Sempere – § 6 – Am 2

explanation: This amendment would have added a new paragraph to the resolution stating that the EU cannot act as democracy guarantor while its funding withholdings, unequal standards, and communication practices might influence Member States’ domestic politics. A Yes vote would have formally approved that addition to the European Parliament’s position.
sourceTitle: A new strategy for media literacy and digital learning
title: Marcos Ros Sempere – After § 6 – Am 3

explanation: The European Parliament's amendment would have required the EU's executive, the European Commission, to propose a new legal act establishing a European Digital Literacy Centre. A Yes vote would have approved this binding request for the Commission to draft and present that specific legislative proposal.
sourceTitle: A new strategy for media literacy and digital learning
title: Marcos Ros Sempere – § 9

explanation: The European Parliament's report on media literacy would have been amended to add a new paragraph 6a. A Yes vote would have added text stressing that the EU cannot present itself as a democracy guarantor while its actions might influence domestic political debates, and that EU institutions must fully respect transparency, equal treatment, neutrality and Member States' democratic self-determination.
sourceTitle: A new strategy for media literacy and digital learning
title: Marcos Ros Sempere – § 10 – Am 4

explanation: A Yes vote would have added a formal invitation for the European Board for Media Services to use its structured dialogue to monitor large online platforms' media literacy actions and increase dialogue between media services and platforms [citation:5].
sourceTitle: A new strategy for media literacy and digital learning
title: Marcos Ros Sempere – § 14

explanation: The amendment would have added a new requirement for Member States and the Commission to develop specific indicators measuring critical thinking as part of media literacy education, alongside existing digital skills benchmarks. A Yes vote would have approved the European Parliament’s formal recommendation for the Commission to propose binding minimum standards for media literacy across all EU countries by 2028.
sourceTitle: A new strategy for media literacy and digital learning
title: Marcos Ros Sempere – § 16/2

explanation: A Yes vote on paragraph 27, second part, would have approved the call for the European Commission to evaluate the Audiovisual Media Services Directive and potentially propose a clear common EU approach for age-appropriate access to online platforms, especially social media, based on protecting children's well-being[citation:11]. This vote concerned a specific part of the resolution on media literacy and digital learning, as introduced by rapporteur Marcos Ros Sempere[citation:3][citation:4].
sourceTitle: A new strategy for media literacy and digital learning
title: Marcos Ros Sempere – § 27/2

explanation: The European Parliament would have changed its non-binding resolution on media literacy by adding a warning that the EU’s Democracy Shield initiative must not be used to promote a single official view of information. A Yes vote would have formally approved this addition, expressing concern that such measures could marginalise opinions critical of EU policies.
sourceTitle: A new strategy for media literacy and digital learning
title: Marcos Ros Sempere – After § 33 – Am 5

explanation: A Yes vote would have amended the European Parliament's own-initiative report on media literacy by adding new text to paragraph 35. This addition would have called on the European Commission and Member States to allocate specific funding and technical support for teacher training in digital skills.
sourceTitle: A new strategy for media literacy and digital learning
title: Marcos Ros Sempere – § 35

explanation: The European Parliament would have required its own members to complete annual media-literacy training, funded from its internal budget for members' allowances. A Yes vote would have approved making that training compulsory for every MEP.
sourceTitle: A new strategy for media literacy and digital learning
title: Marcos Ros Sempere – § 43/2

displayTitle: Final vote on the motion for a resolution
explanation: A Yes vote would approve a resolution calling on the European Commission and member states to prioritize high-quality independent journalism, public service media, and media literacy in a new EU digital learning strategy.
sourceTitle: A new strategy for media literacy and digital learning
title: Marcos Ros Sempere – Motion for a resolution (as a whole)

discussion.speaker: Roberta METSOLA (President)
discussion.text: The next vote is on the implementation and delivery of the Sustainable Development Goals in view of the 2026 High-Level Political Forum (see minutes, item 7.18).

discussion.speaker: Lukas MANDL
discussion.text:
Madam President, colleagues, the United Nations are more needed now than in decades before. The world needs the United Nations. At the same time, the United Nations need a reform. There is an urgent need for a reform.

I thank the co-negotiators here in the European Parliament, especially Pierfrancesco Maran, for tough negotiations, but constructive negotiations to receive a good result for next week's high-level political forum at the UN headquarters in New York to represent the European stance for a rule-based international order.

And I also want to say to some who criticised the Sustainable Development Goals: we have to see them holistically. We have to see them balanced and we have to follow them in a balanced approach. Also, economic growth is part of the Sustainable Development Goals. Also education. Also innovation that drives the economy is part of the SDGs. So if we follow the SDGs in an unideological way and follow them in a balanced way in our operative work, we contribute to a positive outcome.

discussion.speaker: Pierfrancesco MARAN
discussion.text:
Madam President, dear colleagues, sustainability, competitiveness and social justice must go hand in hand. More than a decade ago, the world came together to adopt the 2030 agenda. Since then, millions have escaped poverty and gained access to education, clean water and electricity. Yet today, progress is slowing as conflict and climate change put those achievements at risk.

Next week, at the United Nations High‑Level Political Forum, Parliament will contribute to accelerating the implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals. Leadership means responsibility. Europe must lead by example by advancing climate neutrality, affordable clean energy and stronger international partnership.

displayTitle: Implementation and delivery of the Sustainable Development Goals in view of the 2026 High-Level Political Forum
sourceTitle: Implementation and delivery of the Sustainable Development Goals in view of the 2026 High-Level Political Forum
title: Implementation and delivery of the Sustainable Development Goals in view of the 2026 High-Level Political Forum

displayTitle: Final vote on the motion for a resolution
explanation: A Yes vote would have approved the European Parliament's entire own-initiative resolution on implementing the Sustainable Development Goals ahead of the 2026 UN High-Level Political Forum. This would have formally set out Parliament's full position on EU and member state actions regarding those global goals.
sourceTitle: Implementation and delivery of the Sustainable Development Goals in view of the 2026 High-Level Political Forum
title: Lukas Mandl, Pierfrancesco Maran – Motion for a resolution (as a whole)

explanation: The European Parliament's resolution called on the European Commission to assess whether crypto lending, staking, NFTs, and DeFi should be brought under the EU's regulatory framework, while also supporting euro-denominated stablecoins [citation:1].
